parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Redesign the work around a person
parts.body:
A tool launch changes a job only when the team changes its workflow. Map the old path from intake through decision, correction, and appeal. Then place AI at a specific step and state what the worker sees, checks, edits, and records. Name who is accountable for the final result and what happens when the tool is unavailable. A vague instruction to 'keep a human in the loop' does not tell that person which evidence to inspect or whether they have time and authority to override the output.

Assess the new path at the outcome level. Drafting may fall from 30 minutes to five, but checking figures and correcting omissions may consume 12 more. The 13 minutes released could clear a backlog; it is not automatically a staffing saving. Also inspect whether review becomes harder as employees see fewer examples handled from scratch. Give workers a channel to report failures without penalty and use those reports to revise the process.

Managers need a realistic workload and quality target. If incentives reward volume alone, staff may rubber-stamp AI output. Review a sample of accepted, edited, and rejected outputs, then compare downstream rework and customer outcomes. Adoption is meaningful when eligible work uses the revised path and meets its quality standard.

example.title: A weekly report
example.body: An analyst once spent 30 minutes assembling and writing a report. An assistant drafts in five minutes; the analyst takes nine minutes to verify source figures and four to explain an unusual movement. Net time is 18 minutes. The analyst signs the report and sends missing-data cases back to the data owner.

exercise.title: Draw the revised workflow
exercise.body: For a familiar task, list intake, AI output, human checks, exceptions, approval, record, and fallback. Estimate time at each step and name the person who may override the tool. Identify one skill the worker might lose and how you will maintain it.

sources: OECD: adoption of AI in firms and workforce implications
NIST AI RMF Core: human oversight, feedback, and monitoring

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Teach judgment in context
parts.body:
AI literacy is more than learning where the prompt box is. A worker needs to understand the tool's approved purpose, data boundaries, common failure patterns, how to check an output, and when to escalate. A manager needs to interpret adoption, error, and workload measures. Executives need to ask what evidence supports a scale decision and who can stop a harmful use. Use the actual workflow and examples from its evaluation, with sensitive details removed.

In the EU, the AI Act contains an AI literacy provision for providers and deployers; its application and any amendments should be checked against current official text and guidance for the relevant organization. The Commission's Q&A emphasizes context, staff experience, and the people affected. Canada's federal Directive on Automated Decision-Making is a public-sector instrument for covered federal institutions, not a blanket rule for every Canadian business. It illustrates how role-specific training and documented oversight may matter in consequential automated decisions.

Have staff practice rejecting a plausible but unsupported output. An assessment should ask them to identify a missing source, correct a false claim, and use the escalation route. Count competence demonstrated in the workflow, rather than certificates alone.

example.title: A reviewer exercise
example.body: Give a service worker a draft response that cites a policy page correctly but applies it to the wrong customer category. The worker must identify the mismatch, find the applicable source, correct the answer, and log the error for evaluation. A successful prompt alone would miss this failure.

exercise.title: Create role-specific checks
exercise.body: Write one practical assessment each for an end user, manager, and release owner. Include a failure case, expected response, and evidence that each person understands the approved boundary. Ask local legal or compliance owners to review jurisdiction-specific training needs.

sources: European Commission: AI literacy questions and answers
OECD: bridging the AI skills gap

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Measure adoption with correction cost
parts.body:
A login count cannot tell whether the new workflow is useful. Measure eligible cases, cases where the tool was offered, cases where it was used, correct completed outcomes, corrections, escalations, time, and user feedback. Give each a denominator and segment by team or case type. If usage rises while corrections rise faster, investigate quality, workload, or incentive pressure before celebrating adoption. If people avoid the tool, ask whether the output is poor, the interface slows them, or management has failed to explain its purpose.

Bring employees and affected stakeholders into review where appropriate. Front-line workers often see failure modes that the pilot dataset missed. Encourage specific reports with an example, model or workflow version, consequence, and suggested remedy. Protect privacy and access controls in that feedback channel. NIST's risk framework includes input from users and mechanisms for override, change management, and ongoing monitoring.

Set a change cadence: weekly review during early rollout, then a slower cadence if stable. A new model, data source, or policy may require renewed training and evaluation. Record when an instruction changed and who acknowledged it. If the old workflow remains available, monitor its use to understand exceptions rather than treating fallback as disobedience.

example.title: Usage is not the conclusion
example.body: In an illustrative month, tool use rises from 50% to 80% of eligible cases while manual correction grows from 10% to 25% of used cases. The manager samples corrections and finds a policy change missing from retrieval. The team updates the source and retests before expanding to another region.

exercise.title: Design a weekly adoption review
exercise.body: Choose four outcome and process measures with denominators, a sampling plan for errors, and a feedback route. Define who investigates a rise in corrections and the decision that could pause the rollout.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: Manage 4.1 and monitoring
OECD: adoption of AI in firms

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Negotiate the workforce transition
parts.body:
A CAIO should bring HR, operations, employee representatives where applicable, risk owners, and managers into the redesign early. Explain which tasks will change, what checking time remains, how performance will be measured, what training and backfill are funded, and who will review effects on workload and service. Do not promise that all released time is a saving while simultaneously assigning new checking and exception duties.

Plan for uneven effects. Routine work may become faster while difficult cases become a larger share of each worker's day. Some employees may gain analytical work; others may need support with new tools. Record a baseline for workload, quality, employee experience, and customer outcomes, then review it after deployment. Employment and consultation obligations differ across countries and sectors; local HR and legal teams should apply the relevant agreements and rules.

A transition memo should be candid about uncertainty. Set a pilot population, training plan, protected time for reviewers, employee feedback mechanism, decision date, and conditions for changing workload targets. The business executive owns the staffing decision. The CAIO supplies AI evidence and coordinates the controls, rather than quietly making personnel commitments.

example.title: A manager's launch note
example.body: For eight weeks, an illustrative service team will use an assistant on low-complexity tickets. Staff receive two hours of practice and 15 minutes per shift for feedback. The manager will review time to resolution, correction burden, reopen rate, and employee workload before revising productivity targets. A fallback remains available.

exercise.title: Draft a transition memo
exercise.body: Write 200 words for a team whose workflow will change. Name the changed tasks, training, checking time, measures, employee feedback route, fallback, and who decides on staffing. Include one concern a worker might raise and how the pilot will examine it.

sources: OECD: bridging the AI skills gap
